title: Inverting & Summing Amplifiers
description: Analyse and design inverting amplifiers and summers using the virtual ground.

study.title: The inverting amplifier
study.body: The input drives the − input through $R_1$, $R_2$ feeds the output back to the − input, and the + input is grounded. The summing-point constraint makes the − input a **virtual ground** ($v_- = 0$), so $i_1 = v_{in}/R_1$. No current enters the op amp, so $i_1$ flows on through $R_2$ and $v_o = -R_2 i_1$.

study.title: Input and output resistance
study.body: The source sees $R_1$ connected to a virtual ground, so $R_{in} = R_1$. The output is independent of $R_L$, so $R_{out} = 0$. A source resistance $R_s$ simply adds to $R_1$: $v_o = -\frac{R_2}{R_s+R_1}v_s$, so choose $R_1 \gg R_s$ when $R_s$ is uncertain.

study.title: Summing amplifier
study.body: Several inputs, each through its own resistor, feed the same virtual-ground node. Their currents add and all flow through $R_f$. Each input sees only its own resistor ($R_{in,k} = R_k$), so the inputs do not interact. With all resistors equal, $v_o = -(v_1+v_2+\dots)$; with $R_f = R/n$ the output is minus the average.

study.title: Designing to a gain
study.body: Choose $R_1$ from the input-resistance requirement, then $R_2 = |A_v|R_1$. Keep resistors roughly between 1 kΩ and 1 MΩ: too small and the op amp must deliver large currents, too large and the circuit picks up noise and suffers from bias currents. Use standard values (E12: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82 × $10^n$). Example: $A_v = -4.7$ → $R_1$ = 10 kΩ, $R_2$ = 47 kΩ.

study.title: Tolerances and pitfalls
study.body: With 5 % resistors, $R_2/R_1$ can be off by about ±10 % (one high, the other low); use 1 % parts or a trimmer for tighter gain. The output is inverted (180° phase shift) and must stay inside the saturation limits: $|v_{in}| \le V_{sat}R_1/R_2$. The virtual ground is at 0 V but is **not** connected to ground: never short it in your analysis.

steps.title: Virtual ground
steps.body:
The + input is grounded and negative feedback goes through $R_2$ to the − input. By the summing-point constraint $v_- = v_+ = 0$: the − input is a **virtual ground**.
So the whole input voltage sits across $R_1$: $i_1 = v_{in}/R_1$.

steps.prompt: Why must the current $i_1$ through $R_1$ also flow through $R_2$?
options: No current flows into the op-amp input
steps.explanation: KCL at the − input: $i_1$ arrives, and the ideal op amp has infinite input impedance, so $i_- = 0$. The only path left is through $R_2$: $i_2 = i_1$.

steps.title: The gain
steps.body:
With $i_2 = i_1 = v_{in}/R_1$ flowing through $R_2$ from the 0 V node toward the output, KVL gives $v_o = 0 - R_2 i_2$:
$v_o = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}v_{in}$
The gain is set only by a resistor ratio, and the minus sign means the output is inverted.

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier uses $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. Find the voltage gain $A_v = v_o/v_{in}$.
steps.explanation: $A_v = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}$ = −{{R2|Ω}}/{{R1|Ω}} = {{-R2/R1}}. Don't forget the minus sign.

steps.prompt: With $v_{in}$ = {{vin|V}}, $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, find $v_o$.
steps.explanation: $v_o = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}v_{in}$ = −({{R2|Ω}}/{{R1|Ω}}) × ({{vin|V}}) = {{-R2*vin/R1|V}}. The output has the opposite sign of the input.

steps.title: Input and output resistance
steps.body:
- The source sees $R_1$ ending at a virtual ground: $R_{in} = v_{in}/i_1 = R_1$.
- $v_o = -(R_2/R_1)v_{in}$ does not depend on the load: $R_{out} = 0$, the output acts like an ideal voltage source.

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier has $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. What input resistance does the signal source see?
steps.explanation: The − input is a virtual ground, so the source sees just $R_1$ to (virtual) ground: $R_{in} = R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}. $R_2$ does not appear because the voltage across it is set by the op-amp output, not by the source.

steps.prompt: In an ideal inverting amplifier, doubling the load resistance $R_L$ doubles the output voltage.
steps.explanation: False. $v_o = -(R_2/R_1)v_{in}$ contains no $R_L$: the output resistance is zero, so the output voltage is the same for any load (as long as the op amp can supply the current).

steps.title: The summing amplifier
steps.body:
Connect several inputs, each through its own resistor, to the virtual-ground node. Each input current is $v_k/R_k$; they add up and all flow through $R_f$:
$v_o = -R_f\left(\frac{v_1}{R_1} + \frac{v_2}{R_2}\right)$

steps.prompt: Summing amplifier with an ideal op amp. Tap the resistor that sets the input resistance seen by the source $v_2$.
steps.explanation:
The − input is a virtual ground (0 V). So source $v_2$ sees only $R_b$, from its terminal to a point at 0 V:
$$R_{in,2} = \frac{v_2}{i_2} = R_b$$
$R_a$ belongs to the other input, and the feedback resistor $R_c$ sets the gain $-R_c/R_b$ for $v_2$ but not the input resistance. Because of the virtual ground the inputs do not load each other.

steps.prompt: A summer has $R_1$ = {{RA|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{RB|Ω}} and $R_f$ = {{Rf|Ω}}. The inputs are $v_1$ = {{vA|V}} and $v_2$ = {{vB|V}}. Find $v_o$.
steps.explanation:
Input currents into the virtual ground: $v_1/R_1$ = {{vA/RA|A}}, $v_2/R_2$ = {{vB/RB|A}}.
$v_o = -R_f\left(\frac{v_1}{R_1}+\frac{v_2}{R_2}\right)$ = −{{Rf|Ω}} × ({{vA/RA+vB/RB|A}}) = {{vo|V}}.

steps.prompt: A three-input summer: $v_1$ = {{v1|V}}, $v_2$ = {{v2|V}}, $v_3$ = {{v3|V}}. The resistors are shown in the schematic. Find $v_o$.
You want a three-input summer with $v_o = -(v_1 + v_2 + v_3)$. How should the resistors be chosen?
steps.explanation: Each weight is $R_f/R_k$, so all weights equal 1 when every input resistor equals $R_f$. $R_f = 3R$ would give $-3(v_1+v_2+v_3)$, and $R_f = R/3$ gives minus the average.

steps.prompt: In a summer with $R_1$ = {{RA|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{RB|Ω}}, $v_1$ = {{vA|V}} and $v_2$ = {{vB|V}}, find the current $i_f$ in $R_f$, taken positive when it flows from the − input toward the output.
steps.explanation:
Both input currents flow into the virtual ground (0 V) and none enters the op amp, so KCL gives
$i_f = \frac{v_1}{R_1} + \frac{v_2}{R_2}$ = {{vA/RA|A}} + {{vB/RB|A}} = {{vA/RA + vB/RB|A}}.
Note that $R_f$ does not affect this current; it only sets $v_o = -R_f i_f$.

steps.prompt: In an ideal summing amplifier, changing $v_2$ changes the current drawn from source $v_1$.
steps.explanation: False. Source $v_1$ sees $R_1$ ending at the virtual ground, which stays at 0 V whatever $v_2$ does. So $i_1 = v_1/R_1$ is unaffected: the inputs are isolated from each other, which is why summers make good audio mixers.

steps.prompt: Design a summer with $v_o = -({{a}}v_1 + {{b}}v_2)$. You choose $R_1$ = {{RA|Ω}}. What value is needed for $R_2$?
An averaging circuit uses a summer with {{n}} inputs, each through $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. What feedback resistor $R_f$ makes $v_o$ equal to minus the average of the inputs?
steps.explanation: Each weight is $R_f/R$; the average needs weights of $1/{{n}}$. So $R_f = R/{{n}}$ = {{R|Ω}}/{{n}} = {{R/n|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Ideal op amp. Tap every resistor whose current also flows through the feedback resistor $R_c$.
steps.explanation:
No current enters the op-amp inputs, so KCL at the − input gives $i_c = i_a + i_b$: the currents of both input resistors $R_a$ and $R_b$ continue through $R_c$.
- $R_d$ connects the + input to ground; no input current means no current in $R_d$ (it is there to balance bias currents in a real op amp).
- $R_e$ is the load. Its current comes from the op-amp output, not from $R_c$.

steps.prompt: Design an inverting amplifier with gain −{{G}} and an input resistance of {{X|Ω}}. What value of $R_2$ is needed?
Which resistor pair is the best choice for an inverting amplifier with $A_v = -4.7$?
steps.explanation: The gain is $-R_2/R_1$, so $R_2 = 4.7R_1$ (the reversed pair gives −0.213). 10 Ω/47 Ω would make the source and the op-amp output supply very large currents, and 10 MΩ/47 MΩ is prone to noise pickup, leakage and bias-current errors. Kilo-ohm values are the sweet spot.

steps.prompt: A transducer with internal voltage $v_s$ and internal resistance $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}} drives an inverting amplifier with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. Find $v_o/v_s$.
steps.explanation:
$R_s$ is in series with $R_1$ on the way to the virtual ground, so the input current is $v_s/(R_s+R_1)$.
$\frac{v_o}{v_s} = -\frac{R_2}{R_s+R_1}$ = −{{R2|Ω}}/({{Rs|Ω}} + {{R1|Ω}}) = {{-R2/(Rs+R1)}} (instead of the nominal {{-R2/R1}}).

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier uses 5 % resistors with nominal values $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. What is the **largest** possible gain magnitude $|A_v|$?
steps.explanation:
$|A_v| = R_2/R_1$ is largest when $R_2$ is 5 % high and $R_1$ is 5 % low:
$|A_v|_{max} = \frac{1.05 R_2}{0.95 R_1}$ = {{1.05*R2|Ω}}/{{0.95*R1|Ω}} = {{R2*1.05/(R1*0.95)}}, about 10.5 % above the nominal {{R2/R1}}.

steps.prompt: Two inverting amplifiers are cascaded. Stage 1: $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. Stage 2: $R_3$ = {{R3|Ω}}, $R_4$ = {{R4|Ω}}. Find the overall gain $v_o/v_{in}$.
steps.explanation:
Stage gains: $A_1 = -R_2/R_1$ = {{-R2/R1}} and $A_2 = -R_4/R_3$ = {{-R4/R3}}. Because each stage has zero output resistance, there is no loading between stages.
$A_v = A_1A_2$ = ({{-R2/R1}}) × ({{-R4/R3}}) = {{(R2/R1)*(R4/R3)}}. Two inversions give a positive gain.

steps.prompt: To get $v_o = +k_1v_1 - k_2v_2$, signal $v_1$ first passes through a unity-gain inverter, then both $-v_1$ and $v_2$ go into a summer with $R_A$ = {{RA|Ω}} (for $-v_1$), $R_B$ = {{RB|Ω}} (for $v_2$) and $R_f$ = {{Rf|Ω}}. With $v_1$ = {{v1|V}} and $v_2$ = {{v2|V}}, find $v_o$.
steps.explanation:
The inverter outputs $-v_1$ = {{-v1|V}}.
Summer: $v_o = -R_f\left(\frac{-v_1}{R_A} + \frac{v_2}{R_B}\right) = \frac{R_f}{R_A}v_1 - \frac{R_f}{R_B}v_2$
= {{Rf/RA}} × {{v1}} − {{Rf/RB}} × {{v2}} = {{Rf*(v1/RA - v2/RB)|V}}.

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} uses an op amp whose output saturates at ±{{Vs|V}}. What is the largest input amplitude that avoids clipping?

An inverting amplifier has $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{G*R1|Ω}}. Its input is the dashed sine wave with an amplitude of {{Vm|V}}. Which graph shows the output $v_o$ (solid)? All graphs use the same scale.
steps.explanation: $A_v = -R_2/R_1$ = −{{G}}: the output is the input multiplied by {{G}} and turned upside down, an amplitude of {{G*Vm|V}} with a peak exactly where the input has a valley. A resistive amplifier does not shift the waveform in time, so a cosine-shaped output is wrong, and the gain is {{G}}, not 1.

steps.prompt: The dashed curve is the input and the solid curve the output of an inverting amplifier with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}. Find $R_2$.
steps.explanation: Read the peaks: the input reaches {{Vm|V}}, the output {{G*Vm|V}}, upside down. So $A_v$ = −{{G*Vm|V}} / {{Vm|V}} = −{{G}}. With $A_v = -R_2/R_1$: $R_2$ = {{G}} × {{R1|Ω}} = {{G*R1|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: A summing amplifier with $R_1 = R_2 = R_f$ adds a sine wave $v_1$ with an amplitude of {{Vm|V}} and a dc voltage $v_2$. The graph shows the output. Find $v_2$ (with its sign).
steps.explanation: With equal resistors $v_o = -(v_1 + v_2)$. The sine averages to zero, so the centre line of the output equals $-v_2$. The output swings between {{-V2-Vm|V}} and {{-V2+Vm|V}}, centred on {{-V2|V}}, so $v_2$ = {{V2|V}}.

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier with gain −{{G}} is driven by a sine wave with an amplitude of {{Vm|V}}; the graph shows its output. What is the largest input amplitude that would **not** be clipped?
steps.explanation: The flat tops show the saturation limits: ±{{Vsat|V}}. The output stays undistorted as long as {{G}} × $|v_{in}|$ ≤ {{Vsat|V}}, so the largest amplitude is {{Vsat|V}} / {{G}} = {{Vsat/G|V}}. The {{Vm|V}} input would need an output of {{G*Vm|V}}, which is why it is clipped.

steps.prompt: The dashed curve is the input of an op-amp circuit and the solid curve its output. Which circuit is it?
steps.explanation: Compare phase and amplitude. Upside down: inverting amplifier ($A_v = -R_2/R_1$). Same phase and larger: noninverting amplifier ($A_v = 1 + R_2/R_1 > 1$). Identical to the input, so the two curves lie on top of each other: voltage follower ($A_v$ = 1). Here $A_v$ = {{A}}.
